title: Decision Reviews
description: Learn how to conduct effective reviews of past technical decisions to improve future decision-making and catch problems before they become costly.

data.text: Every technical decision is a bet. Sometimes the bet pays off. Sometimes it does not. Decision reviews are how teams learn from both outcomes. By examining past decisions with honesty and curiosity, teams improve their judgment, catch drift before it becomes crisis, and build a culture where learning is valued over blame.

A good decision review focuses on the process, not the person. The goal is to understand what information was available, what assumptions were made, and what the team would do differently with the benefit of hindsight. This turns isolated events into organizational learning.

Review decisions at predictable intervals rather than waiting for a crisis. Schedule lightweight reviews quarterly for major decisions and after any significant change in context — a new business priority, a team change, a technology shift, or a production incident. The best reviews happen before problems escalate, not after.

data.title: Decision Review Triggers
data.content: Events that should trigger a decision review.
data.code:
Scheduled Reviews:
- Quarterly: Review all architectural decisions from the past quarter
- After onboarding: Review decisions older than 1 year when new engineers join
- Annual: Deep review of the most significant architectural bets

Trigger-Based Reviews:
- Production incident that traces back to a past decision
- Significant change in business requirements
- Team structure changes (new team, reorg, new leadership)
- Technology changes (new framework release, cloud provider change)
- Cost overruns or performance degradation

data.text: A decision review should be lightweight but substantive. Gather the original decision document, current metrics, and the people involved. Walk through what was decided, what actually happened, and why the outcomes differed from expectations. End with concrete actions: update the decision document, plan a course correction, or close the review with a note about what was learned.

items: Gather context: original RFC or ADR, current metrics, incident reports
Reconstruct the decision: what was known, what was assumed, what was decided
Compare outcomes: what actually happened vs. what was expected
Identify gaps: which assumptions were wrong, which risks materialized
Determine action: update documentation, plan a fix, or document the learning

data.text: Not all reviews happen after bad outcomes. Reviewing successful decisions is just as valuable. A decision that worked might have worked for the wrong reasons. Maybe the team got lucky, or maybe the problem was easier than expected. Understanding why a decision succeeded prevents overconfidence and helps replicate the process.

data.title: Survivorship Bias
data.text: Teams tend to review failed decisions more than successful ones. This creates survivorship bias: the team thinks its process is better than it is. Review good decisions with the same rigor as bad ones to avoid overconfidence.
Decision reviews lead to four common outcomes. Understanding these categories helps the team know what to expect and how to act on the results.

items: The decision was right and the execution was right. Celebrate, document the learning, and move on.
The decision was right but the execution was wrong. Fix the execution and document what went wrong during implementation.
The decision was wrong but the execution was right. The system worked despite a poor choice. Plan a course correction.
The decision was wrong and the execution was wrong. Learn from both. Document the failure mode and adjust the decision-making process.

data.text: Decision reviews only work if the team feels safe being honest. If reviews become blame sessions, people will hide problems and justify past decisions instead of learning. Leaders set the tone by sharing their own mistakes, asking curious questions, and rewarding people who surface uncomfortable truths.

terms.definition: A structured examination of a past technical decision to understand its outcomes and improve future decision-making.
The tendency to focus on successful outcomes while ignoring failed ones, leading to overestimation of success likelihood.
A review of an incident or decision that focuses on learning rather than blame.

data.title: Avoid Blame Culture
data.text: If the first question in a review is "who made this decision?" the team has already failed. The right question is "what information did we have, and what would we do differently?"

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Review decisions at predictable intervals and after significant context changes
Focus on the decision process, not individual blame
Review both good and bad decisions to avoid survivorship bias
Document outcomes and update decision records with new information
Create a culture where honest review is safe and valued
Turn every review into a concrete action or documented learning
data.takeaway: Decision reviews transform experience into institutional knowledge. Teams that review their decisions regularly make better ones over time.
